extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, moral psychology, and anthropology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition from a philosophical treatise on how moral character and intellect are transmitted across generations, the physiological and social conditions affecting inheritance, and the metaphysics of the sexual drive. Presents empirical examples, caveats, and practical/political implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character inherited from the father (paternal will)
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual's moral character (the will, inclinations, passions) is transmitted from the father to descendants — fundamental traits of paternal character tend to reappear in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: paternity uncertainty ('pater semper incertus') means only clear physical resemblance removes doubt; superficial resemblance is insufficient and after-effects (e.g., resemblance to a previous husband) occur. The author illustrates with historical and anecdotal examples (e.g., 'The Liar and his Son', P. Decius Mus and his son, the gens Claudia producing Tiberius/Caligula/Nero, Scipios, Cæsar Borgia, Henry VIII → Bloody Mary). Use such examples as empirical support but note observational limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellect inherited from the mother (maternal mind / 'mother-wit')
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual faculties (reason, memory, mental endowments) are primarily inherited from the mother — popular proverbs like 'mother-wit' reflect this view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes biographical examples (Joseph II and Maria Theresa; Rousseau on his mother; D'Alembert and Claudine de Tencin; Buffon; Goethe, Kant, Schiller, Bürger, Walter Scott). Note that female achievements are less publicly recorded, so maternal intellectual influence may be under-documented. The author also warns against conflating maternal moral qualities with intellect in reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification of paternal traits by maternal intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Paternal passions and inclinations appear in the son but are modified by the intellect inherited from the mother, producing bridled, concealed, methodical, or systematic manifestations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a father with limited mind + strong passions vs a son with maternal reason produces a different phenomenon (passions are 'bridled' and manifest more secretly). Conversely, maternal inclinations may sometimes not reappear. Use this criterion to explain differences between parent and child despite shared paternal traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on inheritance claims: paternity, historical evidence, and anecdotal bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about hereditary transmission must account for uncertainties: uncertain paternity, the after-effect of earlier impregnation, falsified or partial historical traditions, and the predominance of public (political) actions over private character in historical records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes careful investigation and candid appraisal. Historical examples are convenient because they are publicly known but are impaired by unreliability of tradition and focus on public acts. Apply skepticism and seek corroboration; recognize cases where resemblance may be accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary professions vs genuine intellectual inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Familial continuities in certain sciences or professions often result from early instruction, diligence, patience, and practice (transmission of training and environment) rather than from inherited extraordinary intellectual genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scaligers, Bernouillis, Cassinis, Herschels — families showing succession of competent men due to hereditary business and early training. Distinguish between native faculties (rare genius) and success due to upbringing and repeated access to the father's workshop or trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and temporal factors in inheritance (conception conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing and physiological state at conception affect which parental traits manifest: father's vigor (energetic action of the heart), mother's brain condition, parents' ages, and temporary disturbances can influence a child's capacities; eldest children are more likely to display eminent traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why siblings (including twins) may differ: eldest often superior; disturbances of vital force at conception can prevent appearance of eminent talent; twins show quasi-identity because of similar conditions. Use these physiological considerations to interpret exceptions and sibling differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritability of pathological tendencies (crime, madness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain pathological tendencies (criminal propensity, suicide, madness) show familial aggregation and may be inherited, with some authorities (Esquirol) proposing maternal predominance for certain disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites newspaper reports, annals of crime, and clinical authorities; uses illustrations (families of highway robbers, cases of cannibalism, suicidality) to argue for hereditary tendencies but notes limits of sources. Treat anecdotal criminal pedigrees as suggestive rather than definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/political applications of hereditary theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If paternal character and maternal intellect propagate through generations, public policy and social customs might be adjusted to improve national character and intelligence (e.g., altering dowry practices, discouraging burdens that harm women's brains, or extreme historical punishments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical proposals in the text include giving dowries to the most understanding women rather than those judged most virtuous, abolishing burdens on women's heads to preserve brain health, and radical historical measures (castration as a severe punishment) — presented as speculative or utopian considerations. Treat these as suggested implications rather than normative prescriptions without ethical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating intellects as a mechanism for moral renewal (salvation by generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perpetual renewal of intellects (different mothers giving different intellects to the same paternal will) presents life with ever-new views, thereby providing the will repeated opportunities to affirm or deny life — this arrangement is posited as a basis for moral development or 'salvation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames this as an ethico-metaphysical result: prohibition of incest (brother–sister marriage) is given an explanation in terms of needing different intellects to prevent stagnation of the same will-plus-intellect configuration. Use this to interpret social taboos and the role of sexual reproduction in moral variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of causal explanation: freedom of the will as thing-in-itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Where moral difference cannot be traced to sufficient reasons (origins of divergent characters), the will as thing-in-itself exhibits true freedom and is not subject to the principle of sufficient reason; such cases mark the limit of causal explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats extreme divergence of character (e.g., one philanthropic, another ferocious) as instances where empirical causes fall away and metaphysical freedom must be acknowledged. This is a methodological caveat: not all differences are explainable by heredity or physiology; some reflect the will's noumenal freedom.
